lessons.title: Vacuum evaporation for heat-sensitive compounds
lessons.body: When you boil hibiscus in an open pot, you lose colour, flavour, and vitamin C because heat destroys them. Vacuum evaporation solves this by lowering the boiling point. Water boils at 100Â°C at sea level, but if you reduce the pressure, it boils at 40â60Â°C. At that temperature, anthocyanins (the red pigments) and delicate aromas survive. In Africa, small-scale processors use simple vacuum evaporators made from a stainless steel pot with a sealed lid, a vacuum pump (like a refrigerator compressor) and a condenser. You can also find entry-level rotary evaporators from China for around $500â$1,500. For a start, you can build a DIY vacuum evaporator using a pressure cooker, a vacuum pump, and a copper coil in a bucket of cold water. The process: fill the pot with your hibiscus extract (already filtered), seal it, turn on the vacuum pump, and heat gently to 50Â°C. Water evaporates and is collected in the condenser. You concentrate until the volume is reduced by 70â80%. For example, 10 litres of extract becomes 2â3 litres of thick concentrate. The key is to monitor temperature with a thermometer and keep it below 60Â°C. This method is ideal for making premium concentrate for export or for adding to drinks where you want a fresh, fruity taste. It uses more equipment than open boiling, but the quality difference is huge. In Nigeria and Kenya, some zobo producers use vacuum evaporation to make concentrates that retain the bright red colour and tart taste. Remember: always clean and sanitise your equipment to avoid spoilage. Start with small batches (5â10 litres) to learn the technique before scaling up.

lessons.title: Reverse osmosis and membrane filtration
lessons.body: Reverse osmosis (RO) and membrane filtration are advanced ways to concentrate hibiscus extract without heat. They work by forcing the liquid through a semi-permeable membrane under high pressure. Water passes through, but larger molecules like sugars, acids, and pigments stay behind. This gives you a concentrated extract at room temperature, preserving heat-sensitive compounds perfectly. In Africa, RO systems are common in water treatment, so you can adapt small units. A basic RO system for 50â100 litres per hour costs around $1,000â$3,000. For hibiscus, you first filter the extract through a cloth or coffee filter to remove coarse particles. Then you pass it through the RO membrane. The permeate (water) is discarded, and the retentate (concentrate) is collected. You can achieve concentration up to 20â30% solids, similar to vacuum evaporation but without heat. However, RO membranes can clog with pectin and fine particles, so pre-filtration is critical. Also, you need to clean the membrane regularly with caustic soda and citric acid. Another option is ultrafiltration, which uses a looser membrane to remove proteins and pectin, clarifying the juice. Nanofiltration can separate sugars and acids. For a small business, start with a 100 GPD (gallons per day) RO unit, which costs about $200â$500. You can concentrate 20 litres of extract to 5 litres in a few hours. The downside: RO is slower than boiling and requires electricity and maintenance. But the quality is excellent: the concentrate keeps its fresh taste and bright colour. In South Africa and Egypt, some juice companies use RO for premium products. For a zobo concentrate, RO is a great choice if you have reliable power and can invest in the equipment. Always test your concentrate for microbial stability because RO does not pasteurise.

lessons.title: Freeze concentration principles
lessons.body: Freeze concentration is a gentle method that removes water as ice, leaving behind a concentrated liquid. It works because when you freeze hibiscus extract, water forms pure ice crystals, while sugars, acids, and pigments remain in the unfrozen liquid. You then separate the ice from the concentrate. This process preserves heat-sensitive compounds better than any other method because it uses no heat. In practice, you can do simple freeze concentration at home or in a small workshop using a freezer and a sieve. First, freeze your hibiscus extract in shallow trays overnight. Then, let it partially thaw at room temperature. The first liquid that drips out is the most concentrated. Collect it, and discard the ice. Repeat the freeze-thaw cycle 2â3 times to increase concentration. For example, 10 litres of extract can become 2 litres of concentrate with 4â5 times the original strength. The colour and flavour are almost identical to fresh hibiscus. However, this method is slow and energy-intensive if you use a freezer. For larger scale, you can use a scraped-surface heat exchanger to freeze the liquid into a slurry, then a centrifuge or press to separate ice. Industrial freeze concentrators cost $10,000â$50,000, so they are not for beginners. But you can start with a chest freezer and plastic buckets. A practical tip: add a small amount of sugar (5â10%) to the extract before freezing; it helps form larger ice crystals that are easier to separate. Also, work quickly to avoid microbial growth during thawing. Freeze concentration is ideal for making a premium, all-natural concentrate for health-conscious customers. In Africa, this method is rare but can be a unique selling point. Use it for small batches of high-value product, like organic zobo concentrate for export.

lessons.title: Ultrasound-assisted extraction
lessons.body: Ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) uses sound waves to break open plant cells and release more colour and flavour in less time. A sonicator produces high-frequency sound waves (20â40 kHz) that create tiny bubbles in the liquid. When these bubbles collapse, they generate shock waves that rupture cell walls. This means you can extract more from hibiscus calyces using less solvent and lower temperatures. For example, traditional soaking might take 12â24 hours and extract 60% of the anthocyanins. With UAE, you can achieve 90% extraction in 30â60 minutes at 40Â°C. In Africa, small-scale UAE units are becoming available. A basic ultrasonic bath (like those used for cleaning jewellery) costs $100â$300 and can process 5â10 litres. For larger batches, probe sonicators cost $1,000â$5,000. To use UAE: place dried hibiscus calyces and water (or water with a little citric acid) in the ultrasonic bath. Set the temperature to 40â50Â°C and sonicate for 30â45 minutes. Then filter and concentrate as usual. The extract will be darker, more aromatic, and higher in antioxidants. You can also combine UAE with enzymatic treatment (see next lesson) for even better yields. However, ultrasound can generate heat, so monitor temperature and use an ice bath if needed. Also, the equipment requires electricity and maintenance. For a small business, UAE is a smart investment if you want to increase yield and reduce processing time. In Nigeria, some zobo producers use ultrasonic cleaning baths to speed up extraction. Start with a simple bath and experiment with time and temperature. You will need to filter the extract well because ultrasound can create fine particles. UAE is scalable and can be a competitive advantage.

lessons.title: Enzymatic extraction to increase yield
lessons.body: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. In hibiscus extraction, enzymes like pectinase, cellulase, and hemicellulase break down the plant cell walls, releasing more colour, flavour, and solids. This can increase your yield by 20â40% compared to simple water extraction. For example, if you normally get 5 litres of concentrate from 10 kg of dried hibiscus, with enzymes you might get 6.5â7 litres. The enzymes work under specific conditions: temperature 40â55Â°C, pH 3.5â5.0 (hibiscus is naturally acidic, so pH is often fine), and time 1â3 hours. You can buy food-grade enzyme preparations from suppliers like Novozymes or DSM, but they can be expensive. A cheaper option is to use crude enzyme extracts from local sources: papaya skin (rich in papain), pineapple peels (bromelain), or even a handful of crushed bean sprouts. However, these are less predictable. For consistent results, buy a commercial pectinase blend. Dosage is typically 0.1â0.5% of the fruit weight. So for 10 kg of hibiscus, use 10â50 grams of enzyme powder. Mix the enzyme with a little water, add to your hibiscus mash, and keep warm for 2 hours. Then filter and concentrate. The enzyme treatment also clarifies the juice, making filtration easier. You must inactivate the enzymes after extraction by heating to 80â90Â°C for 5â10 minutes, or they will continue to act and may cause off-flavours. Enzymatic extraction is common in the fruit juice industry in South Africa and Kenya. For a small zobo business, it is a cost-effective way to boost yield and quality. Start with a small trial: treat half your batch with enzyme and compare. You will likely see a noticeable difference in colour and taste.

lessons.title: Workshop: comparing extraction yields and quality
lessons.body: In this workshop, you will compare four extraction methods: traditional boiling, vacuum evaporation, freeze concentration, and ultrasound-assisted extraction. You will measure yield (volume of concentrate), colour intensity (using a simple spectrophotometer or colour chart), taste (sweetness, tartness, aroma), and cost. This will help you choose the best method for your business. First, prepare a large batch of hibiscus extract by soaking 1 kg of dried calyces in 10 litres of water for 4 hours. Divide the extract into four equal parts (2.5 litres each). For traditional boiling, boil one part in an open pot until reduced to 500 ml (5x concentration). For vacuum evaporation, use a vacuum pump and heat at 50Â°C until reduced to 500 ml. For freeze concentration, freeze one part, then thaw and collect the first 500 ml of concentrate. For ultrasound, sonicate one part for 45 minutes at 45Â°C, then filter and boil gently to 500 ml. Record the time and energy used for each. Next, evaluate quality. Measure colour by diluting each concentrate to the same strength and comparing with a colour chart or a smartphone app like Colorimeter. Taste each concentrate diluted in water (1 part concentrate to 4 parts water) and score on a scale of 1â10 for flavour, aroma, and overall acceptability. Also measure total soluble solids with a refractometer (Brix). You will likely find that vacuum evaporation and freeze concentration give the best colour and flavour, but freeze concentration is slowest. Ultrasound gives high yield and good quality but requires equipment. Traditional boiling is cheapest but loses colour and flavour. Calculate the cost per litre of concentrate, including energy and labour. For example, if electricity costs $0.15 per kWh, vacuum evaporation might use 2 kWh ($0.30) per litre, while boiling uses 5 kWh ($0.75). Use this data to decide which method suits your market. If you target premium customers, invest in vacuum or freeze. For bulk sales, traditional may be fine. Share your results with the group and discuss.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Choosing an Extraction & Concentration Route for Hibiscus (Zobo/Sobolo) Concentrate

This practical reference is written for African processors who already make hibiscus (zobo/sobolo) drinks and now want to move from batch boiling to a repeatable, sellable concentrate. The commercial logic is simple: hibiscus calyces are cheap and seasonal; concentrate is expensive and year-round. If you can extract more colour and acid per kilogram of calyx, and remove water without destroying the delicate anthocyanins that give zobo its deep red colour, you protect margin on three fronts â raw material, packaging, and cold-chain.

The five technologies covered in this module â vacuum evaporation, reverse osmosis/membrane filtration, freeze concentration, ultrasound-assisted extraction, and enzymatic extraction â are not competitors. They are stages. A realistic small-to-medium African plant might combine ultrasound-assisted extraction (to shorten maceration and raise yield), enzymatic treatment (to break down pectin and release more colour), membrane filtration (to clarify and pre-concentrate), and vacuum evaporation or freeze concentration (to reach a stable, transportable solids level). This lesson gives you the numbers, the quality trade-offs, and the decision rules to pick a route that matches your capital, your market, and your climate.

How the technologies compare on yield, colour, and cost

Anthocyanins â the pigments responsible for zobo's red colour â degrade with heat, oxygen, and light. The central quality question is therefore: how much heat does your concentration step apply? Vacuum evaporation lowers the boiling point (typically 45â60 Â°C at reduced pressure), which protects colour compared with open-pan boiling but still applies thermal load. Freeze concentration removes water as ice, leaving solutes behind with almost no heat exposure â the best colour retention, but the highest capital and energy cost. Reverse osmosis concentrates at ambient temperature using pressure across a membrane; it is excellent as a pre-concentration step but struggles to reach high solids because osmotic pressure rises. Ultrasound and enzymes act upstream: they increase extraction yield, so less calyx is needed per litre of concentrate.

Table 1. Typical performance ranges for hibiscus extraction and concentration options (indicative; validate with your own trials)
Technology Main effect Typical operating window Expected yield / quality impact Relative capex & energy
Conventional hot-water maceration (baseline) Simple solidâliquid extraction 90â100 Â°C, 30â60 min Baseline yield; highest colour loss Low capex, high energy per kg solids
Ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) Cavitation ruptures cell walls, speeds mass transfer 20â40 kHz, 40â60 Â°C, 10â30 min 10â30 % higher yield; shorter time; better colour retention than boiling Medium capex; lower thermal energy
Enzymatic extraction (pectinase / cellulase) Breaks pectin and cell-wall polysaccharides 0.05â0.2 % w/w enzyme, 40â55 Â°C, 1â3 h 5â20 % higher yield; improved clarity and filterability Low capex; enzyme cost per batch
Reverse osmosis / membrane filtration Ambient-temperature water removal and clarification 20â60 bar; 15â25 Â°Brix achievable Good colour retention; limited final solids; membrane fouling risk Mediumâhigh capex; moderate energy
Vacuum evaporation Boiling under reduced pressure 45â60 Â°C, 0.1â0.3 bar; 50â65 Â°Brix Good colour retention vs open boiling; some anthocyanin loss Mediumâhigh capex; steam/electric demand
Freeze concentration Water removed as ice; solutes retained â5 to â15 Â°C; 40â55 Â°Brix Best colour and aroma retention; highest cost High capex and energy; niche premium products

Sources: ranges compiled from FAO, Fruit and Vegetable Processing (FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 119); FAO/WHO, Codex General Standard for Fruit Juices and Nectars (CODEX STAN 247-2005); and published food-engineering literature on ultrasound- and enzyme-assisted extraction of anthocyanin-rich plant materials. Treat as planning ranges, not guarantees.

What this means for your unit economics

Consider a processor who currently buys 100 kg of dried hibiscus calyx per week and produces a ready-to-drink zobo at roughly 8 Â°Brix. If ultrasound-assisted extraction plus a pectinase step raises extractable solids by 20 %, that same 100 kg now supports 120 kg-equivalent of finished product â or the processor can cut calyx purchases by about 17 % for the same output. At a farm-gate calyx price that fluctuates sharply between harvest and off-season, that is direct margin protection.

Concentration then changes your logistics. Shipping water is the most expensive habit in African beverage supply chains. A 65 Â°Brix concentrate contains roughly one-eighth the water of a single-strength drink. One 20-litre drum of concentrate can be diluted on-site into hundreds of litres of finished zobo, which means you can serve distributors in Lagos, Nairobi, or Accra from one central plant without paying to truck water. The table below shows the arithmetic.

Table 2. Indicative mass balance: 100 kg dried hibiscus calyx to concentrate (illustrative, based on 50â65 Â°Brix target)
Step Input Output Notes
Extraction (water + calyx) 100 kg calyx + 800 L water ~850 L extract at 3â5 Â°Brix UAE/enzyme can raise soluble solids recovery
Clarification ~850 L extract ~800 L clarified extract + solids waste Waste can be composted or used as animal feed
Pre-concentration (RO) ~800 L at 4 Â°Brix ~200 L at 15â20 Â°Brix Ambient temperature; protects colour
Final concentration (vacuum or freeze) ~200 L at 15â20 Â°Brix ~55â65 L at 55â65 Â°Brix Vacuum: 45â60 Â°C. Freeze: â5 to â15 Â°C
Packaging ~55â65 L concentrate ~55â65 L packed concentrate Hot-fill or aseptic; dilute 1:6 to 1:8 for drinking

Sources: mass-balance approach adapted from FAO, Fruit and Vegetable Processing (FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 119) and FAO, Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing and Products (FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 127). Brix and yield figures are planning estimates; confirm with laboratory analysis of your own calyx variety and water quality.

â  SAFETY WARNING â pressure, heat, and process hygiene

Reverse osmosis and membrane systems operate at 20â60 bar. Never open, adjust, or service a pressurised membrane housing without isolating the pump, depressurising the line, and following the manufacturer's lock-out/tag-out procedure. Vacuum evaporators combine hot surfaces with vessels under negative pressure; a failure to break vacuum before opening can cause scalding or implosion. Freeze concentrators use refrigerants and low-temperature surfaces â ensure refrigerant handling is done only by certified technicians and that ice-slurry lines cannot contact skin. Enzymatic extraction uses protein powders that can cause respiratory sensitisation: wear a dust mask and eye protection when weighing enzymes, and never reuse enzyme containers for food. Finally, hibiscus extract is an acidic, sugar-rich medium â sanitise all contact surfaces and validate your hot-fill or aseptic step against a recognised microbiological standard before selling concentrate.

Decision rules for African processors

If you are starting up with limited capital: begin with ultrasound-assisted extraction and a food-grade pectinase. Both are relatively low-capex, improve yield immediately, and reduce the amount of calyx you need. Concentrate using a simple vacuum evaporator if you can source one; if not, sell single-strength chilled zobo locally while you build capital.

If you are supplying distributors across borders: invest in reverse osmosis as a pre-concentration step, then vacuum evaporation to 55â65 Â°Brix. This combination gives you a stable, shippable concentrate at a fraction of the water weight, and the RO step protects colour before the thermal step.

If you are targeting premium export or health-food buyers: freeze concentration is the quality leader. It preserves anthocyanins and aroma compounds better than any thermal route. The trade-off is capital and energy, so it only makes sense if your selling price supports it â typically in branded, high-value concentrates rather than commodity drums.

Regardless of route: measure. Track Â°Brix, pH, colour (absorbance at ~520 nm for anthocyanins), and microbial counts at every batch. A cheap refractometer and pH meter will pay for themselves in the first month by catching under-concentration and spoilage risk before product leaves the gate.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Calyx quality: buy dry, deep-red calyces with low foreign matter; reject mouldy or faded lots before they enter extraction.
  • Water: use potable water with low iron and chlorine; iron dulls anthocyanin colour and chlorine adds off-flavours.
  • Extraction: combine ultrasound (20â40 kHz) with a pectinase step at 40â55 Â°C to raise yield and cut maceration time.
  • Clarification: centrifuge or membrane-filter before concentration to reduce fouling and improve final clarity.
  • Concentration: match the method to your market â vacuum for mainstream, RO for pre-concentration, freeze for premium colour retention.
  • Target solids: aim for 55â65 Â°Brix for shelf-stable concentrate; verify with a calibrated refractometer each batch.
  • Safety: depressurise membrane systems, break vacuum before opening evaporators, and wear dust protection when handling enzymes.
  • Record-keeping: log Â°Brix, pH, colour absorbance, batch yield, and sanitation checks â this data is your pricing and compliance evidence.

Further Reading (free official sources)

  • FAO, Fruit and Vegetable Processing â FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 119. Free at fao.org (chapters on juice extraction, evaporation, and membrane concentration).
  • FAO, Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing and Products â FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 127. Free at fao.org.
  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius, General Standard for Fruit Juices and Nectars (CODEX STAN 247-2005). Free at fao.org.
  • FAO, Code of Hygienic Practice for Low and Acidified Low Acid Canned Foods (CXC 23-1979). Free at fao.org.
  • FAO, Processing of Fruits and Vegetables for Small-scale Enterprise â free FAO agribusiness training materials at fao.org.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills course on Hibiscus (Zobo/Sobolo) Drink Concentrate. Use these figures as a starting point for your own trials, and always validate food-safety and quality parameters with a qualified food technologist before commercial sale.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of vacuum evaporation for hibiscus concentrate?
options: A) It is the cheapest method
D) It produces the highest yield
quiz.explanation: Vacuum evaporation lowers the boiling point, so heat-sensitive compounds like anthocyanins are preserved.

quiz.q: At what temperature does water boil under vacuum in a typical vacuum evaporator?
quiz.explanation: Under reduced pressure, water boils at 40â60Â°C, which is gentle on heat-sensitive compounds.

quiz.q: Which equipment is essential for vacuum evaporation?
options: A) A vacuum pump and a sealed pot
B) A freezer and a sieve
quiz.explanation: Vacuum evaporation requires a vacuum pump to reduce pressure and a sealed vessel to hold the extract.

quiz.q: What is a common DIY vacuum pump source for small-scale processors?
quiz.explanation: Refrigerator compressors are often repurposed as vacuum pumps for small-scale evaporation.

quiz.q: How much can vacuum evaporation reduce the volume of hibiscus extract?
quiz.explanation: Vacuum evaporation can concentrate the extract by removing 70â80% of the water.

quiz.q: What is the principle behind reverse osmosis for concentration?
options: B) Using sound waves to break cells
C) Forcing liquid through a membrane under pressure
quiz.explanation: Reverse osmosis uses pressure to push water through a semi-permeable membrane, leaving concentrated solutes behind.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key maintenance step for RO membranes?
options: B) Cleaning with caustic soda and citric acid
quiz.explanation: RO membranes must be cleaned regularly with caustic soda and citric acid to prevent clogging.

quiz.q: What is a major disadvantage of reverse osmosis for small-scale hibiscus concentrate production?
options: B) It requires electricity and maintenance
quiz.explanation: RO systems need reliable electricity and regular maintenance, which can be a challenge in some areas.

quiz.q: What is the typical concentration factor achieved by reverse osmosis for fruit juices?
quiz.explanation: RO can concentrate juices up to 20â30% solids, similar to vacuum evaporation.

quiz.q: Which membrane process is used to clarify juice by removing proteins and pectin?
quiz.explanation: Ultrafiltration uses a looser membrane to remove larger molecules like proteins and pectin.

quiz.q: What is the basic principle of freeze concentration?
options: A) Water freezes into pure ice, leaving concentrated liquid
B) Sugars freeze first, leaving water
C) Heat is used to evaporate water
D) Pressure forces water through a membrane
quiz.explanation: When the extract freezes, water forms ice crystals while sugars, acids, and pigments remain in the liquid.

quiz.q: How can you perform simple freeze concentration at home?
options: B) Freeze the extract, then partially thaw and collect the first liquid
D) Add salt to the extract
quiz.explanation: Freeze-thaw cycles allow you to separate the concentrated liquid from the ice.

quiz.q: What is a practical tip to improve freeze concentration?
quiz.explanation: Adding 5â10% sugar helps form larger ice crystals that are easier to separate.

quiz.q: Why is freeze concentration considered gentle?
quiz.explanation: Freeze concentration uses no heat, so heat-sensitive compounds are preserved.

quiz.q: What is a drawback of freeze concentration for large-scale production?
options: B) It is energy-intensive and slow
quiz.explanation: Freeze concentration is slow and energy-intensive, especially if using a freezer.

quiz.q: How does ultrasound-assisted extraction work?
options: A) It uses sound waves to create bubbles that rupture cell walls
B) It uses high pressure to force water through membranes
C) It uses enzymes to break down pectin
D) It uses freezing to separate water
quiz.explanation: Ultrasound creates cavitation bubbles that collapse and generate shock waves, breaking plant cells.

quiz.q: What frequency range is typical for ultrasound-assisted extraction?
quiz.explanation: Most UAE systems operate at 20â40 kHz for optimal cavitation.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of UAE compared to traditional soaking?
options: C) It increases yield and reduces time
quiz.explanation: UAE can increase extraction yield and reduce processing time from hours to minutes.

quiz.q: What is a common small-scale ultrasound device?
quiz.explanation: Both ultrasonic baths and probe sonicators are used, with baths being cheaper for small scale.

quiz.q: What precaution should you take when using UAE?
options: A) Monitor temperature to avoid overheating
B) Add oil to the extract
quiz.explanation: Ultrasound can generate heat, so temperature should be monitored and controlled.

quiz.q: What role do enzymes play in hibiscus extraction?
options: A) They break down cell walls to release more compounds
quiz.explanation: Enzymes like pectinase and cellulase degrade plant cell walls, improving extraction yield.

quiz.q: Which enzyme is commonly used to break down pectin in fruit extraction?
quiz.explanation: Pectinase is widely used to break down pectin, which helps release juice and colour.

quiz.q: What is the typical dosage of commercial enzyme for hibiscus extraction?
quiz.explanation: Enzyme dosage is usually 0.1â0.5% of the weight of the plant material.

quiz.q: Why must enzymes be inactivated after extraction?
options: A) To prevent off-flavours and further reaction
quiz.explanation: Inactivation stops enzymatic activity that could cause undesirable changes in flavour or colour.

quiz.q: What is a cheap local source of enzymes for extraction?
quiz.explanation: Papaya skin (papain) and pineapple peels (bromelain) are natural sources of enzymes.

quiz.q: In the workshop, what is a key parameter to measure when comparing extraction methods?
quiz.explanation: Yield, colour, taste, and cost are all important for comparing methods.

quiz.q: Which extraction method is likely to give the best colour and flavour retention?
quiz.explanation: Vacuum evaporation and freeze concentration both avoid high heat, preserving colour and flavour.

quiz.q: What instrument is used to measure total soluble solids in the workshop?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures Brix, which indicates total soluble solids.

quiz.q: What is a cost consideration when choosing an extraction method?
quiz.explanation: Energy, equipment, and labour all contribute to the cost per litre of concentrate.

quiz.q: Which method is generally the cheapest but lowest quality?
quiz.explanation: Traditional boiling is inexpensive but destroys heat-sensitive compounds, reducing quality.
